cues.text: A House That Became a Church
John Mark , as the New Testament calls him, was the son of a Jerusalem woman named Mary.
Her own house served as a gathering place for the earliest Christian community.
It was to this very house that Peter came, we are told, immediately after his miraculous release from prison, finding the disciples already assembled there in prayer for him.
Mark was also a cousin of Barnabas .
This family connection first drew the young man into the company of Paul and Barnabas, who took him with them to Antioch.
When the two set out on the Church's first great missionary journey, they brought him along as their assistant.
A Failure, and a Second Chance
Partway through that first journey, at Perga in Pamphylia, Mark abandoned the mission and returned home to Jerusalem, for reasons Scripture does not record.
Paul regarded Mark's departure as sufficiently serious that he did not wish to take him on the next journey, although Scripture does not explain Mark's reasons or characterize his motives.
When Paul and Barnabas later prepared for a second journey, their disagreement over Mark’s reliability grew sharp enough to divide the two great missionaries entirely.
Paul refused to bring the young man again, but Barnabas, true to his own name and character, insisted on giving him another chance.
The two parted ways, Barnabas taking Mark with him back to Cyprus — a quiet act of patient encouragement whose fruit the whole Church would eventually inherit.
Interpreter of Peter
Mark's later years brought him into close association with St. Peter , who refers to him with evident affection as "my son" in his own first epistle.
Ancient and remarkably consistent testimony, beginning with the early second-century bishop Papias, holds that Mark served as Peter's interpreter in Rome.
It also holds that his Gospel represents, in substance, Peter's own preaching about Jesus, set down carefully in writing after the great Apostle's death.
This tradition explains much about the character of Mark's Gospel: its vivid, almost eyewitness immediacy and its unflinching honesty about the disciples' own frequent misunderstanding and fear.
Its rapid, urgent pace is propelled again and again by the word "immediately" — the voice, many have suggested, of Peter's own blunt, unadorned memory of walking with the Lord.
A Second Redemption Confirmed
Even Paul's own earlier verdict on Mark's reliability was thoroughly reversed by the end of both their lives.
In his final letters, written from a Roman prison shortly before his martyrdom, Paul instructs Timothy to bring Mark with him.
He adds that Mark is "very useful to me for ministry."
Through patient formation and a second chance freely given, the young man once judged unfit became indispensable to the Apostle who had refused to travel with him.
Founder of the Church of Alexandria
Constant tradition, both Eastern and Western, credits Mark with carrying the Gospel to Egypt and founding there the great Church of Alexandria .
He became its first bishop, establishing a Christian community that would grow into one of the most important sees of the ancient world.
It eventually gave rise to the Coptic Orthodox Church, which honors Mark to this day as its founder and continues to trace its own line of patriarchs directly back to him.
Legacy
Tradition holds that Mark was martyred in Alexandria, dragged through the city's streets by an enraged pagan mob.
His relics were later carried to Venice, where the great Basilica of San Marco was raised in his honor.
There, his winged lion became the emblem of the city itself.
The young man who once turned back partway through a journey became, through the patient faith of one relative and the mercy of a second chance, the author of the Church's first written Gospel.

He also became the founder of one of Christianity's oldest and most enduring sees—a life that continues to assure every believer who has ever failed at something important that God's plans are rarely finished by a single stumble.
